items.summary: 活动预告｜国际组织十讲：联合国大学全球治理工作坊 AI Social GameTh 清华大学人工智能国际治理研究院 2026-10-17 20:40 分享 以下文章来源于mp.weixin.qq.com 点击蓝字，关注清华大学国际教育 “国际组织十讲”系列讲座系统介绍并分析国际组织在全球各重大议题中扮演的角色与发挥的作用。作为国际组织入门引导，面向清华大学全体学生开放。 2026年10月20日-21日 ，联合国大学全球治理系列工作坊将邀请 联合国大学日内瓦政策研究中心主任 Adam Day 博士 担任主讲，聚焦联合国改革、复杂性全球治理、气候治理、AI治理等核心议题，开展 为期两天、六个模块的线下工作坊 ，深度解读全球治理领域的前沿研究与变革趋势。 本次系列讲座是 系统学习和研讨全球治理前沿议题 的绝佳机会，欢迎报名！ 活动信息 系列讲座时间地点 10月20日 周二 清华大学国际交流中心（新清华学堂零层） 10月21日 周三 清华大学北院 报名方式 请扫描单场讲座对应的雨课堂二维码进行报名； 如报名多场讲座，每场均需单独扫码。 主讲嘉宾 Adam Day 联合国大学日内瓦政策研究中心主任 Adam Day博士现任联合国大学日内瓦政策研究中心主任，同时担任哥伦比亚大学国际公共事务学院兼职副教授、日内瓦研究生院客座讲师、伦敦国王学院战争研究系客座高级研究员。他拥有伦敦国王学院战争研究系博士学位，以及塔夫茨大学、加州大学伯克利分校、布朗大学等校的法学、外交与比较文学硕士学位，具备跨学科学术背景。 Adam Day博士拥有十余年联合国维和行动一线经验，曾担任联合国刚果（金）稳定特派团高级政治顾问，在苏丹、黎巴嫩、中东、北非等地及联合国总部承担政治顾问与政策制定工作。他深度参与联合国改革与多边治理，担任联合国秘书长科学咨询委员会研究负责人、联合国有效多边主义高级别咨询委员会秘书处联合负责人，主导多项重大政策研究。其研究聚焦全球治理、冲突解决、复杂性理论、气候安全等领域，出版《永恒危机》等多部专著，学术成果与实践经验兼具国际影响力。 具体安排 10月20日13:00 - 14:30 The UN in Crisis: Reforming the UN for the 21st Century 联合国的困境与改革：面向21世纪的联合国转型 10月20日14:45 - 16:15

items.content: Developer Tools & Techniques Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile Oct 19, 2026 By Sylvain Gugger , Axel Feldmann , Yinuo Liu and Siddharth Samsi Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model that abstracts thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives to automatically target Tensor Cores and other advanced GPU hardware features. Machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented the Mamba-2 state-space model in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize three custom kernels for the forward pass: chunk_cumsum, fwd_pass_state, and compute_out. The chunk_cumsum kernel computes per-token, per-head cumulative sums of the decay term in log-space using ct.cumsum, storing results for reuse by the subsequent kernels. The fwd_pass_state kernel uses ct.mma to execute Tensor Core matrix-multiply operations that advance the hidden state across sequence chunks, applying the jump formula with exponential decay and pre-multiplied operands. The compute_out kernel fuses the carried-state term, the decayed and causally masked interaction matrix, and the skip connection into a single tiled kernel that keeps intermediate matrices in registers and casts to TF32 for Tensor Core execution. Performance optimizations include latency hints for DRAM traffic modeling, operand swapping to route fused operands to Tensor Memory, transposed memory layouts for TMA-friendly access, and an autotuner that searches block size and occupancy parameters for each input shape. Next Steps Get started with cuTile to write high-performance GPU kernels in Python. Explore the cuTile Python documentation for API details and usage guides. Review cuTile Python GitHub repositories for source code and contribution information. Examine sample code to see practical kernel implementations. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them. Overview and prerequisites To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. Sequence modeling computational trade-off Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Mamba-2 architecture The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is: \(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\) y t = c t ⊤ h t + D x t y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t Where: \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\) \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\) \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply: \(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\) This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores. An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just: \(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\) If building a matrix \(B\) of shape ( T, S ) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape ( T, H ) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\): Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula. Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute: \(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\) Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this: Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention). When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection): \(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) With \(M\) the traditional causal mask. Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like: \(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\) Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability. Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe This will translate into three kernels: chunk_cumsum : Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk. fwd_pass_state : Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above. compute_out : Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step. Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk. The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay a and a per-token timestep dt . The effective decay at token t for head h is a[h] * dt[t, h] , and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute exp2 instead of exp , the result is scaled by log2(e) . This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use: ct.bid , ct.load / ct.store , and ct.cumsum . The full kernel is short: @ct.kernel def chunk_cumsum_kernel( a: torch.Tensor, # [num_heads] dt: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] output: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] chunk_size: ct.Constant[int], BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int], ) -> None: chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,), shape=(BLOCK_H,), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype)) The kernel is launched with a grid of (num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size) , the first line determines where you are in the grid using ct.bid . The broadcast product of a_tile (shape [BLOCK_H] ) and dt_tile (shape [1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H] ) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile. ct.cumsum(..., axis=1) then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by fwd_pass_state and compute_out . Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state fwd_pass_state computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that compute_ou t will later project into outputs. At its core, the kernel is a sequential loop over chunks as described earlier. Each kernel launch loads one (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice, hid_tile has a shape [BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE] and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk. head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group hid_tile = ct.load( init_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) In each iteration of the loop, first store the hidden state: num_chunks = ct.cdiv(b.shape[1], chunk_size) for chunk_idx in range(num_chunks): ct.store( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)).astype(hiddens.dtype), ) The rest of the loop loads one chunk of x , b , dt , and decay_cumsum to compute the next chunk’s initial hidden state. As shown previously, the math is: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) ct.extract enables taking the last token from the decay tile loaded (to compute \(G_last\)). Each kernel launch owns one (batch, chunk, head, head_tile) output tile and works in two phases. Phase 1 loops over state tiles, using ct.mma to build the interaction matrix cb_tile = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state term C @ H.T at the same time. chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group cb_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, chunk_size), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) out_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) # Phase 1: build CB = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state output for state_tile_idx in range(state_size // BLOCK_STATE): b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) c_tile = ct.load( c, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) h_tile = ct.load( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) cb_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, b_tile.transpose(), cb_tile) out_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, h_tile.transpose().astype(c_tile.dtype), out_tile) Phase 2 applies the decay and causal mask to cb_tile ( ct.arange and ct.where build the lower-triangular mask M , so no mask tensor is ever materialized) and then adds all of the terms to get the final output tile. Both accumulators start as ct.full register tiles, and the final ct.mma casts to ct.tfloat32 to run through the Tensor Cores at near-FP32 accuracy. # Phase 2: decay + causal mask then final computation d_tile = ct.load(decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) x_tile = ct.load(x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) d_val = ct.load(d, index=(head,), shape=(1,)) cb_tile = cb_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) # pairwise decay idx = ct.arange(chunk_size, dtype=ct.int32) cb_tile = ct.where(idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :], cb_tile, 0.0) # causal mask out_tile = out_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None]) # decay carried state dt_x = dt_tile[:, None] * x_tile out_tile = ct.mma(cb_tile.astype(ct.tfloat32), dt_x.astype(ct.tfloat32), out_tile) out_tile = out_tile + d_val * x_tile # D * x skip ct.store(out, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), tile=out_tile.reshape((1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD)).astype(out.dtype)) As mentioned, while some numerical unstable exponentials are computed in the ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) line (some of those are positive numbers), immediately mask them out so potential overflows don’t end up poisoning the computation. The compiler leverages these hints to optimize instruction scheduling and pipeline buffer depth. Learn more NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). The broadcast product of a_tile (shape [BLOCK_H] ) and dt_tile (shape [1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H] ) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile. ct.cumsum(..., axis=1) then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by fwd_pass_state and compute_out . Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state fwd_pass_state computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that compute_ou t will later project into outputs. At its core, the kernel is a sequential loop over chunks as described earlier. Each kernel launch loads one (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice, hid_tile has a shape [BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE] and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk. head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group hid_tile = ct.load( init_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) In each iteration of the loop, first store the hidden state: num_chunks = ct.cdiv(b.shape[1], chunk_size) for chunk_idx in range(num_chunks): ct.store( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)).astype(hiddens.dtype), ) The rest of the loop loads one chunk of x , b , dt , and decay_cumsum to compute the next chunk’s initial hidden state. As shown previously, the math is: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) ct.extract enables taking the last token from the decay tile loaded (to compute \(G_last\)). Use exp2 instead of exp for performance reasons, as shown previously. ct.mma is the API that will execute the matrix-multiply add while leveraging the Tensor Cores. x_tile = ct.load( x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) dt_tile = ct.load( dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_tile = ct.load( decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_last = ct.extract(d_tile, index=(chunk_size - 1,), shape=(1,)) b_dt_d = b_tile * (dt_tile * ct.exp2(d_last - d_tile))[:, None] hid_tile = ct.exp2(d_last) * hid_tile hid_tile = ct.mma(x_tile.transpose(), b_dt_d.astype(b.dtype), hid_tile) After the final chunk, hid_tile contains the final hidden state, which is stored. During inference this value can be fed back as the next call’s init_state ; during training it is usually discarded. ct.store( final_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)), ) The sequential dependence stays inside a single grid point (program instance), while the independent (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slices run in parallel across the grid. Kernel 3: compute_out compute_out is the final kernel in the forward pass. It takes the per-chunk initial hidden states produced by fwd_pass_state and computes the token outputs, implementing the output equation derived earlier: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) A direct PyTorch implementation would compute these three terms separately, materializing the full [B, n_chunks, chunk_size, chunk_size] interaction matrix C @ B.T in global memory. compute_out fuses them into one tiled kernel and keeps that matrix in registers. Each kernel launch owns one (batch, chunk, head, head_tile) output tile and works in two phases. Phase 1 loops over state tiles, using ct.mma to build the interaction matrix cb_tile = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state term C @ H.T at the same time. chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group cb_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, chunk_size), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) out_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) # Phase 1: build CB = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state output for state_tile_idx in range(state_size // BLOCK_STATE): b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) c_tile = ct.load( c, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) h_tile = ct.load( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) cb_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, b_tile.transpose(), cb_tile) out_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, h_tile.transpose().astype(c_tile.dtype), out_tile) Phase 2 applies the decay and causal mask to cb_tile ( ct.arange and ct.where build the lower-triangular mask M , so no mask tensor is ever materialized) and then adds all of the terms to get the final output tile. Both accumulators start as ct.full register tiles, and the final ct.mma casts to ct.tfloat32 to run through the Tensor Cores at near-FP32 accuracy. # Phase 2: decay + causal mask then final computation d_tile = ct.load(decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) x_tile = ct.load(x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) d_val = ct.load(d, index=(head,), shape=(1,)) cb_tile = cb_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) # pairwise decay idx = ct.arange(chunk_size, dtype=ct.int32) cb_tile = ct.where(idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :], cb_tile, 0.0) # causal mask out_tile = out_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None]) # decay carried state dt_x = dt_tile[:, None] * x_tile out_tile = ct.mma(cb_tile.astype(ct.tfloat32), dt_x.astype(ct.tfloat32), out_tile) out_tile = out_tile + d_val * x_tile # D * x skip ct.store(out, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), tile=out_tile.reshape((1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD)).astype(out.dtype)) As mentioned, while some numerical unstable exponentials are computed in the ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) line (some of those are positive numbers), immediately mask them out so potential overflows don’t end up poisoning the computation. Mamba-2 performance optimization With the Mamba-2 workload defined in the cuTile-Python DSL, several key performance optimizations are introduced: Latency hint: cuTile allows you to annotate ct.load and ct.store operations with latency hints to model DRAM traffic. The compiler leverages these hints to optimize instruction scheduling and pipeline buffer depth. Swap A/B: On the NVIDIA Blackwell fifth-generation Tensor Core, MMA operands are asymmetric: operand A can live in Tensor Memory, but operand B must live in Shared Memory. For an input-fusion pattern like the SIMT-op + Dot-op in fwd_pass_state , the identity \(B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = (AB)^{\mathsf{T}}\) is used to route the fused operand ( b_dt_d ) to operand A, relieving shared-memory contention. GMEM layout: The default strided memory access for decay_cumsum and dt lowers to cache-unfriendly LDG instructions. Transposing to a [batch, head, token] layout ensures contiguous access, enabling the use of TMA. cuTile-Python autotuner: Since performance bottlenecks shift with input shape, no single optimization strategy fits every model configuration. These optimizations are integrated alongside cuTile parameters ( block_size , occupancy) into a unified search space, leveraging cuTile exhaustive_search to automatically find the optimal setup for each input shape. Mamba-2 forward pass performance benchmarks This implementation of the Mamba-2 forward pass kernel is available through TileGym . A complete example is shown below. import torch import tilegym from tests import common from tests.ops.test_mamba2 import Mamba2ProblemSpec tilegym.set_backend("cutile") num_tokens, state_size = 16384, 128 torch.manual_seed(0) spec = Mamba2ProblemSpec(batch_size=4, num_tokens=num_tokens, num_groups=1, num_heads=8, state_size=state_size, head_size=64, chunk_size=128, dtype=torch.bfloat16, state_dtype=torch.float32) fwd_inputs = spec.get_sample_inputs(with_reference=False, with_backward=False) fwd = common.benchmark( lambda: tilegym.ops.mamba2_chunk_forward(**fwd_inputs), use_cupti=True, ) print(f"Forward: {fwd['forward']['median'] * 1000:.2f} us") The performance of the implemented Mamba-2 forward pass was evaluated against an open source implementation of the Mamba-2 kernel written in Triton, under the following software and hardware configurations: Software mamba_ssm 2.3.2.post1 (NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton reference), Triton 3.7.1 cuTile: cuda-tile 1.5.0 TileIR assembler ( tileiras ) 13.4 PyTorch 2.13.0, CUDA 13.3 (Driver and Runtime API, NVCC V13.3.33), Driver 595.58.03 cuda-python / cuda-bindings 13.3.1 Python 3.12.3, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-107 Hardware Single NVIDIA B300 SXM6, compute capability 10.3 (NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra) 1920 MHz max SM clock, 1100 W power limit, 268 GiB HBM Figure 5. Performance of cuTile Mamba-2 forward pass The results show that the optimized cuTile forward-pass kernels are 1.14x to 1.82x faster, with speedups growing as sequence lengths and state size increases. Note that these are kernel-level speedups only and end-to-end training results will also depend on the backward pass implementations. Get started with cuTile cuTile enables you to write clear, readable, and highly performant kernels in Python. Stay tuned for a follow-up post describing how the backward pass is implemented in cuTile. Get started with cuTile and explore the documentation , GitHub repos , and sample code . items.content: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More Surviving the perfect storm: how hardware PMs can beat the AI tax and trade tariffs Akash Rathi Mind The Product (2026) Preview Preview abstract This piece analyzes how hardware product managers can navigate the financial pressure of AI-related costs and trade tariffs. It presents a practical framework for deploying the Joint Development Model (JDM) as a product development strategy to balance innovation with cost efficiency, enabling sustainable growth for next-generation AI-native consumer devices. View details One Attack to Rule Them All: Tight Quadratic Bounds for Adaptive Queries on Cardinality Sketches Edith Cohen Jelani Nelson Tamas Sarlos Mihir Singhal Uri Stemmer SODA 2026 Preview Preview abstract Cardinality sketches are compact data structures for representing sets or vectors. These sketches are space-efficient, typically requiring only logarithmic storage in the input size, and enable approximation of cardinality (or the number of nonzero entries). A crucial property in applications is \emph{composability} of the sketching map, meaning that the sketch of a union of sets can be computed from individual sketches. Existing designs provide strong statistical guarantees, ensuring that a randomly sampled sketching map is accurate with high probability for a number of queries that is exponential in the sketch size $k$. However, these guarantees degrade to quadratic in $k$ when queries are adaptive, meaning they depend on previous responses. Prior works on statistical queries (Steinke and Ullman, 2015) and specific MinHash cardinality sketches (Ahmadian and Cohen, 2024) established that this is tight in that they can be compromised using $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ adaptive queries. In this work, we develop a unified attack framework that applies to broad classes of cardinality sketches. We show that any union-composable sketching map can be compromised with $\tilde{O}(k^4)$ adaptive queries. Moreover, this improves to a tight bound of $\tilde{O}(k^2)$ for monotone composable maps (special cases include MinHash, statistical queries, Boolean linear maps), for any linear map over the reals $\mathbb{R}$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_p$, and for any linear map over the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ but when the estimator may only use the nonzero structure of the sketch (as in Cormode et al., 2003). Our work is the first to apply to general composable maps and establishes and builds on fundamental properties of these structures. Specifically for linear sketches, we are the first to establish tight quadratic bounds, to any subclass, and our bounds strengthen weaker polynomial bounds recently established by Gribelyuk et al. (2024). View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details A simple and efficient implementation of strong call by need by an abstract machine Małgorzata Biernacka Witold Charatonik Tomasz Drab Journal of Functional Programming, Volume 36 (2026) Preview Preview abstract We present an abstract machine for a strong call-by-need strategy in the lambda calculus. The machine has been derived automatically from a higher-order evaluator that uses the technique of memothunks to implement laziness. The derivation has been done with the use of an off-the-shelf transformation tool implementing the "functional correspondence" between higher-order interpreters and abstract machines, and it yields a simple and concise description of the machine. We prove that the resulting machine conservatively extends the lazy version of Krivine machine for the weak call-by-need strategy, and that it simulates the normal-order strategy in bilinear number of steps. View details Rational Area Profiles of Regular Polygons Cut by Two Congruent Diagonals Keiichi Watanabe Shoichi Inoue 2026 Preview Preview abstract Regular-polygon geometry is tightly linked to cyclotomic arithmetic: Poonen and Rubinstein’s treatment of three-diagonal concurrence, for example, turns a geometric incidence condition into a short vanishing sum of roots of unity. We prove an analogous rigidity result for areas. Two congruent crossing diagonals divide a regular n-gon into four regions. For the four regions cut out by the two congruent crossing diagonals V0Vm and VkVn−m+k of a regular n-gon, we completely classify, for all parameters (n, k, m), which sums of the normalized areas a0, . . . , a3 are rational. The classification has a sharp finite–infinite contrast: a0 is rational in only five configurations, whereas the rational cases for a2 and adjacent two-region sums form infinite families. Rationality is delicately sensitive to the parameters: for the configuration (14, 3, 5), no nontrivial subset sum is rational, while the neighboring cut (14, 4, 5) gives a2 = 5/7. The proof reduces each rationality condition to trigonometric relations at rational multiples of π and combines cyclotomic norm arguments with the classification theorems of Conway–Jones and Poonen–Rubinstein. See opportunities

items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: Featured projects With Helion’s release last year, it aimed at enabling developers to write GPU kernels in PyTorch-native Python and let its powerful autotuner do the work that used to require hand-written Triton and abstract away hardware-specific implementation details. Helion’s autotuner explores thousands of kernel configurations and routinely lands within a few percent of expert-tuned code, and oftentimes exceeding it. The question that now needs to be answered is this: If a kernel has already been autotuned and optimized to the best of a developer’s ability, is there anything left? There is. It lives below the kernel, in the compiler. Every kernel autotuner in the ecosystem whether it is Helion’s, Triton’s, the one inside torch.compile, they all search the same thing: tile shapes, warp counts, pipeline stages, memory access strategy. All of those are decisions about what work each thread block does. Underneath them sits a second set of decisions about how that work becomes machine assembly instructions generated by ptxas, NVIDIA’s PTX assembler. Things like register allocation policy, fine-grained instruction scheduling, code-generation heuristics are left at their defaults for all kernels shipping today – not because the defaults are optimal, but because nothing was searching and optimizing them! Helion now enables this, and this post is about what that second compiler-specific space contains, why searching it jointly with the kernel configuration space shows further improvements on kernels that were already deemed to be optimal. The searching is done by NVIDIA’s CompileIQ, which optimizes ptxas controls the way an autotuner optimizes tile sizes and packages the result as a portable Advanced Control File (ACF). Most users won’t run that search themselves: CompileIQ publishes pre-tuned ACF catalogs that Helion’s autotuner can now evaluate alongside the kernel configurations it already explores. Starting off with highly-optimized kernels & optimizing the last-mile It matters a great deal what baseline one compares against. A “we made kernels faster” claim is easy if the starting point is a naive kernel, and close to meaningless for real-world workloads. The kernels we use here come from the pretuned_kernels/ in the Helion repository, roughly 27 kernels covering the shapes that show up in real model code: FP8 and NVFP4 quantization, RMSNorm variants, RoPE, grouped GEMM, causal depthwise convolution, Gated DeltaNet decode, and fused model regions like a Qwen3 decode layer. The important property to note here is that these are not autotuned on the fly. Each one ships with ahead-of-time heuristic files per architecture: _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm90.py for H100, _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm100.py for B200 etc. that Helion selects at runtime. The autotuning search already happened offline, and its result is baked in. When this program is run, the user gets tuned performance with no search cost. That is our baseline: a kernel whose configuration space has already been swept, on the hardware it’s running on, by the kernel authors and the Helion compiler developers. If there’s headroom below that, it’s real headroom and that’s the last-mile focus of this post. What Helion’s autotuner searches, and where it stops A Helion kernel is ordinary PyTorch with one new idea – tiles: import torch, helion, helion.language as hl @helion.kernel() def softmax(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: n, _m = x.size() out = torch.empty_like(x) for tile_n in hl.tile(n): out[tile_n, :] = torch.nn.functional.softmax(x[tile_n, :], dim=1) return out The user never says how big a tile is. That’s the point: hl.tile declares that the iteration space is tiled, and the autotuner decides the rest. A single kernel definition implicitly generates a search space of thousands of Triton configurations that span block_sizes, loop_orders, l2_grouping, num_warps, num_stages, indexing (pointer arithmetic vs. block pointers vs. TMA descriptors), pid_type, reduction_loops, and more. Helion lowers through TorchInductor to Triton, compiles each candidate, times it, and keeps the winner. Then the winning Triton kernel goes to ptxas, and everything from that point down happens at PTXAS’ default settings. The kernel autotuner’s search space is defined by what the kernel language can express, and no kernel language expresses “allocate registers differently”. This compiler control surface is a separate interface, exposed by ptxas itself starting from CUDA 13.3. It is imperative to mention that this exploration is genuinely hard. There are complex interactions between various compiler controls: a change to register allocation shifts occupancy, which changes whether a scheduling decision helps or hurts. The right setting is workload-specific, and there’s no universal answer to publish. And the payoff per unit of human effort is poor, which is exactly the profile of a problem one hands off to a search algorithm. The joint search: Helion Autotuner and PTXAS’ Advanced Controls Helion exposes the underlying compiler control space through two settings. Controls are packaged in an Advanced Control File (ACF, typically ending with .acf) which is a binary artifact applied at compile time, portable and versionable, that users can ship alongside their kernel. The first setting pins a known-good ACF as part of a config the user has already chosen: softmax_tuned = helion.kernel( config=helion.Config( advanced_controls_file="h100_example1.acf", block_sizes=[4], num_warps=8, num_stages=2, reduction_loops=[512], indexing=["pointer", "pointer", "tensor_descriptor", "tensor_descriptor", "pointer", "pointer"], ), static_shapes=True, )(_softmax) The second is a more interesting case. It hands a list of ACFs to Helion’s own autotuner and lets them be searched as just another dimension, alongside tile sizes and warp counts: softmax_search = helion.kernel( autotune_search_acf=[ "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_03.acf", "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_11.acf", "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_17.acf", ], autotune_compile_timeout=120, static_shapes=True, )(_softmax) Two things are worth pointing out in this mode: The empty string is appended for you. Helion automatically adds “”, meaning “no ACF, compiler defaults”, to the list that is supplied. The default configuration is therefore always a candidate in the search, and the autotuner will only select an ACF if it actually won on measured time. The worst case of turning this on is that you spend some autotuning budget and get back the kernel you already had. That property is what makes it tempting to try on a kernel you care about. Sequential tuning finds a local optimum; this joint method doesn’t. This is the substantive argument for doing it in one loop rather than two. Suppose you autotune the kernel first, get block_sizes=[128, 128] with num_stages=4, and then go searching for compiler controls. You are now searching the control space conditioned on a kernel config that was itself chosen under default controls. But those dimensions are coupled through the hardware: block size and stage count determine register pressure and shared-memory footprint, and register allocation policy is precisely what decides whether that pressure causes spills. A control set that would shine at block_sizes=[64, 64] never gets evaluated there, because the kernel config was frozen before the compiler search began.The reverse ordering has the same problem. Searching both together is the only ordering that doesn’t have it, which is why autotune_search_acf lives inside Helion’s autotuner rather than being a post-processing step. The cost is search time. Each ACF multiplies the number of compile-and-measure trials, so this is not something to leave on by default for every kernel in a codebase. It is something to run once, offline, on a kernel that matters, and then pin the result with advanced_controls_file, exactly the way autotuned configs are pinned today. Where do these Advanced Control Files come from Now that we’ve understood the benefits of joint autotuning of Helion parameters with PTXAS’ advanced control files (ACF), the natural question one may have is how can these ACFs be generated. That is where NVIDIA’s CompileIQ comes into the picture. CompileIQ treats compiler-control selection as a hyperparameter optimization problem. It pulls a curated search space for the target compiler and toolkit version, then runs an evolutionary search: propose a population of candidate control sets, compile each one, check correctness against a reference, time the survivors, breed the winners, repeat. The output of this search process is an ACF file. There is nothing GPU-specific about the search algorithm itself, and the only GPU-specific parts are what is entirely in the objective function that the user writes, which is usually a few lines around triton.testing.do_bench. For most users however, the additional search budget is unnecessary, because the searching has been done. CompileIQ publishes Booster Packs – pre-tuned ACF catalogs – on its GitHub releases . The current helion-booster-pack contains 24 ACFs tuned across a range of Helion kernels, validated against ptxas from CUDA 13.4, targeting B200. So the realistic workflow for users is: download the pack, point Helion’s autotune_search_acf at it, autotune once, pin what wins. No search space to design, no objective function to write, no compiler expertise required! If you have a workload the pack doesn’t cover, pip install compileiq and run your own targeted search. That path is documented in NVIDIA’s CompileIQ blog post and in various CompileIQ examples . Helion and CompileIQ: Experimental Results This section highlights many possible ways in which one can run a CompileIQ optimization campaign on Helion kernels. As a sample case study we applied CompileIQ to the pretuned nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel, a Helion W4A4 (NVFP4 weight x NVFP4 activation) decode GEMV kernel that already ships a checked-in Helion AOT config for its target shape. The question: is there performance CompileIQ can extract below Helion’s own autotuning layer ,i.e., at the ptxas compilation stage? Environment and Methodology Benchmarking was conducted on a GB200 system with sm_100 (Blackwell, compute capability 10.0), utilizing ptxas 13.3.73 (CUDA 13.3), CompileIQ 1.0.3, Triton 3.8.0, and an editable source installation of Helion. All timing evaluations were executed via triton.testing.do_bench with the GPU clock locked. Every observed performance improvement was re-measured independently, validated against the PyTorch reference implementation for numerical correctness, and statistically filtered using a Welch’s t-test (p < 0.05) alongside Cohen’s d (d > 0.2). Complete statistical metrics are provided alongside each result below. Kernel Description nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel in helion/pretuned_kernels/nvfp4_gemv/nvfp4_gemv.py, computing out = (weight @ x) * alpha for a decode (one output row) GEMV. Both the packed NVFP4 weight and activation bytes are unpacked per K-group via hl.load_float4_e2m1fn_x16_to_float16, accumulated in fp16 over a 16-way static range, and scaled by a decoded E4M3 block scaler. This kernel includes a checked-in AOT configuration specifically for the N=8192, K=28672 “down_proj” decode-GEMV shape in _helion_aot_nvfp4_gemv_cuda_sm100.py: _CONFIG_FP4IN_DEFAULT = { "block_sizes": [4, 256], "num_warps": 2, "num_stages": 3, "range_multi_buffers": [None, True], } Using Runtime as CompileIQ Objective Function Using runtime as the CompileIQ objective function lets us optimize execution speed directly. The objective function takes a candidate ACF configuration, applies it to our fixed Helion kernel, and evaluates it: the kernel runs once, its output is checked against the PyTorch reference implementation, and only configurations that pass correctness are then benchmarked with triton.testing.do_bench. Any configuration that fails correctness returns an invalid score and is dropped from the search before it ever contributes a timing measurement. def objective(config) -> float: acf_path = ... # write `config` to a .acf, or None for baseline kernel = _make_kernel(acf_path) got = run() _check(got, ref, "fp4in", N, K) # correctness gate return do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean") We initialize a Search instance that couples our scoring routine to an evolutionary autotuner over PTXAS compiler controls, then invoke .start(). It sweeps candidate ACFs across generations generations of a pool_size-sized population, breeding the top-performing control configurations forward into each subsequent iteration. config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="min", generations=8, pool_size=15) tuner = Search( objective_function=objective, search_space=PtxasSearchSpace(version=cuda_version, variant="default"), search_config=config, dump_results="nvfp4_gemv_results.csv", worker_type=WorkerTypes.ISOLATED, # crashing ACF candidates shouldn't kill the search ) with gpu_benchmark_mode(clock_mhz=target_clock_mhz, raise_on_failure=False): results = tuner.start(task_timeout=60) Executing an evolutionary search with CompileIQ across PTXAS ACFs, spanning 8 generations with a pool size of 15 candidates over our fixed Helion configuration on GB200 yielded an optimized ACF control set. This candidate reduced execution time from a baseline of 0.0971 ms down to 0.0928 ms, delivering a 1.047x (4.7%) speedup as measured directly within the search’s scoring loop. sample baseline run: 0.09713 ms Best runtime (CompileIQ Search): 0.0928 ms Speedup: 1.047x Validation of CompileIQ Search Results To confirm our findings, every speedup is re-measured independently using increased warmup and repetition iterations under fixed GPU clock frequencies. Each configuration undergoes strict correctness verification against the reference model alongside a Welch’s t-test and Cohen’s d filter. This serves as our rigorous statistical threshold (requiring p < 0.05, cohens_d > 0.2, and optimized.mean < baseline.mean) to verify performance gains before trusting the numbers. # run 1 baseline: n=1744 mean=0.09752ms std=0.00218 optimized: n=2018 mean=0.09301ms std=0.00133 speedup_mean: 1.0485 p_value: 0.0 cohens_d: 2.501 significant: True # run 2 (independent re-run) baseline: n=1757 mean=0.09744ms std=0.00216 optimized: n=2028 mean=0.09299ms std=0.00130 speedup_mean: 1.0478 p_value: 0.0 cohens_d: 2.489 significant: True The two executions remain virtually identical within experimental variance: with d ≈ 2.5 demonstrating a massive effect size that easily surpasses our statistical threshold of 0.2 , verifying that this ACF performance gain is genuine. The two runs are virtually identical within experimental variance, and d ≈ 2.5 in both is a massive effect size nearly 12.5x past our d > 0.2 gate, confirming this ACF performance gain is genuine, not noise. Tuning against a hardware metric instead of runtime While execution speed is a common optimization goal, CompileIQ is not limited to runtime alone. Integrating directly with Nsight Compute (ncu) enables the objective function to target any hardware metric exposed by the tool. To determine the key architectural bottleneck limiting kernel performance, we start by evaluating its profile and analyzing nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel on a GB200 system highlights the following bottlenecks: Section: GPU Speed of Light Throughput Memory Throughput % 78.99 L1/TEX Cache Throughput % 89.35 Compute (SM) Throughput % 37.29 Section: Occupancy Theoretical Occupancy % 25.0 Achieved Occupancy % 21.63 Est. Speedup: 21.01% ... theoretical occupancy (25.0%) is limited by the number of required registers. Profiling shows the kernel is register-limited. NCU’s own cost model attributes a 21% ‘Est. Speedup’ opportunity to occupancy, and this ceiling is set by register count, something PTXAS’s register-allocation controls can directly influence. Switching the objective from runtime to occupancy only touches two things: what the objective function scores, and the search’s problem_type: # objective(): do_bench(...) becomes an ncu metric read return _measure_occupancy(acf_path) # ncu: sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active # search config: minimize runtime -> maximize occupancy config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="max", generations=4, pool_size=6) Pointing the search at achieved occupancy itself across 4 generations × pool size 6, rather than runtime, found a candidate that moved the proxy metric by +0.16pp (21.60% → 21.76% achieved occupancy, p = 9.2e-23, d = 13.17) and, independently re-measured, translated into a modest but statistically solid runtime win of ~1.75-2.0% (p = 3.6e-116, d = 0.78). Multi-Objective Tuning CompileIQ can also perform multi-objective tuning, where the scoring routine evaluates candidates along multiple dimensions simultaneously by returning a tuple rather than a scalar float. Instead of isolating a single top performer, the autotuning process maps out candidates along the Pareto frontier, identifying control sets that are not dominated across all target metrics. This yields a unified ACF optimized jointly for execution runtime alongside L1TEX cache throughput. def objective(config) -> tuple[float, float]: runtime_ms = do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean") l1_throughput = _measure_l1throughput(acf_path) return runtime_ms, -l1_throughput 8 generations × pool size 15 converged to a single dominant candidate on the Pareto front. Unlike a tradeoff curve, this single point beats every other evaluated candidate on both axes simultaneously in the search’s own scoring. Validating it on a fresh cache at shipping-grade trial counts: === RUNTIME (ms, lower is better) === p_value=3.516e-295 cohens_d=87.024 speedup_mean=1.0689x === L1TEX THROUGHPUT (%, higher is better; internally negated) === p_value=7.123e-19 cohens_d=3.686 baseline L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=81.5087% candidate L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=85.9620% Multi-objective tuning found an ACF delivering a validated 6.9% runtime speedup, accompanied by a simultaneous 4.5pp L1TEX throughput gain (81.51% → 85.96%). Both results are statistically significant (p ≪ 0.05, Cohen’s d ≫ 0.2), with neither metric being traded off against the other. Joint ACF Optimization Across Multiple Input Shapes While earlier evaluations focused on a single kernel shape, N=8192, K=28672, real-world model deployment demands coverage across multiple configurations. The nvfp4_gemv implementation ships with several pre-tuned Helion AOT configurations, including a dedicated setup for N=15360, K=5120. Instead of maintaining distinct control files per shape, CompileIQ enables a unified search to discover a single, joint ACF that maximizes performance across both shapes simultaneously. def objective(config) -> tuple[float, ...]: """One shared ACF, one runtime score per shape (both minimize).""" acf_path = ... # write `config` to a temp .acf, or None for baseline return tuple(_bench_shape(acf_path, shape) for shape in SHAPES) Executing an 8-generation search with a pool size of 15 across both shapes yielded a Pareto front containing 4 optimal candidates: Candidate down_proj 15360_5120 pareto_0 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms pareto_1 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms pareto_2 0.0944 ms 0.0308 ms pareto_3 0.0917 ms 0.0321 ms Compared to the default benchmark times of 0.0972 ms for down_proj and 0.0315 ms for 15360_5120, pareto_0 emerges as the standout configuration that consistently outpaces the baseline across both target tensor dimensions. To confirm these performance gains, we execute an independent validation of pareto_0 on each individual shape. Both configurations comfortably pass our statistical validation (1.05x speedup with a p-value of 1.1e-224 and Cohen’s d of 67.71 for down_proj, and 1.01x speedup with a p-value of 6.2e-73 and a d of 4.54 on the 15360_5120 shape), far exceeding our benchmark requirements and proving these gains represent genuine performance improvements rather than system noise. A single joint ACF successfully outperforms the default baseline across both target dimensions simultaneously. Applicability of this workflow for end-to-end model tuning While the focus of this entire post is about optimizing the underlying compiler for extracting more performance from individual kernels, it is important to zoom out and highlight how a workflow like this could be utilized for end-to-end tuning of models on PyTorch. The first step is to profile and characterize the most important kernels that are part of the model which you wish to optimize. Then, each of these kernels can then be a target of CompileIQ optimization, with an associated Advanced Control File to extract maximum performance from that instantiation of the kernel. These get applied during runtime using Helion’s pinned autotune configurations, using Triton’s ptxas_options API or directly via the PTXAS command line depending on the entry point of each kernel’s implementation. We want to be upfront about the expected gains: On kernels that are already highly optimized, compiler-control tuning has shown runtime improvements on the order of 2-7% which may still mean a lot for critical kernels in top models. Less optimized kernels have achieved double-digit performance gains, offering greater potential for meaningful end-to-end improvements. The important points to note are that it is found automatically, and requires little to no compiler expertise, it is verified against your own correctness check, and the result is a file you can commit next to the kernel and reapply on every build. It is the difference between a few percent that exists in principle and a few percent you actually ship. It also compounds exactly where you’d want it to. There are high-value kernels inside inference loops that run continuously across large fleets. Even a few percent at the bottom of the stack, applied to the operations that dominate a decode step, is valuable at that scale. Caveats ACFs are hardware- and toolkit-specific: An ACF tuned for sm_90 is not valid on sm_100. Applying a mismatched ACF can produce incorrect results or runtime errors, not just slower code. The booster pack manifest states its target architecture and toolkit version. This is also why the correctness check in the search loop is not optional. Search-time is a nontrivial cost: Every ACF in autotune_search_acf multiplies your autotuning trials. Use it offline on kernels that matter, then pin the winner. Gains are workload-specific: The result depends on the workload, the shapes, the architecture, and how much headroom the kernel has left. The only number that matters for your kernel is the one you measure on your kernel. Your turn to try this out! If you’ve never written a GPU kernel: start at pretuned_kernels/ . Pick something close to what you need, read it and then run it. The kernels are short, and they run at tuned speed immediately, with no autotuning wait. If you already use Helion: download the helion-booster-pack , add autotune_search_acf=[…] to one kernel you care about, and autotune it. The no-ACF baseline stays in the search, so the downside is bounded at the time you spend. See Helion’s examples/acfs/ for a worked example. If you work on kernels for a living: the takeaway here is not the tool itself. It is that the compiler’s control surface is a legitimate optimization space, it is searchable, and most people are not yet searching it. That is true of any compiler that exposes tunable controls, on any backend. We’re hopeful that we’ve inspired you to explore this space! Licensing Helion is open source and hosted by the PyTorch Foundation. CompileIQ is free to use and it is distributed under the NVIDIA Software License Agreement, a proprietary EULA. The ACF files it produces are freely distributable, which is why booster packs can be published and why an ACF can be committed alongside a kernel in an open repository. Links Helion https://github.com/pytorch/helion https://helionlang.com https://github.com/pytorch/hel
