A “we made kernels faster” claim is easy if the starting point is a naive kernel, and close to meaningless for real-world workloads. The kernels we use here come from the pretuned_kernels/ in the Helion repository, roughly 27 kernels covering the shapes that show up in real model code: FP8 and NVFP4 quantization, RMSNorm variants, RoPE, grouped GEMM, causal depthwise convolution, Gated DeltaNet decode, and fused model regions like a Qwen3 decode layer. The important property to note here is that these are not autotuned on the fly. Each one ships with ahead-of-time heuristic files per architecture: _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm90.py for H100, _helion_aot_rms_norm_cuda_sm100.py for B200 etc. that Helion selects at runtime. The autotuning search already happened offline, and its result is baked in. When this program is run, the user gets tuned performance with no search cost. That is our baseline: a kernel whose configuration space has already been swept, on the hardware it’s running on, by the kernel authors and the Helion compiler developers. If there’s headroom below that, it’s real headroom and that’s the last-mile focus of this post. What Helion’s autotuner searches, and where it stops A Helion kernel is ordinary PyTorch with one new idea – tiles: import torch, helion, helion.language as hl @helion.kernel() def softmax(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: n, _m = x.size() out = torch.empty_like(x) for tile_n in hl.tile(n): out[tile_n, :] = torch.nn.functional.softmax(x[tile_n, :], dim=1) return out The user never says how big a tile is. That’s the point: hl.tile declares that the iteration space is tiled, and the autotuner decides the rest. A single kernel definition implicitly generates a search space of thousands of Triton configurations that span block_sizes, loop_orders, l2_grouping, num_warps, num_stages, indexing (pointer arithmetic vs. block pointers vs. TMA descriptors), pid_type, reduction_loops, and more. Helion lowers through TorchInductor to Triton, compiles each candidate, times it, and keeps the winner. Then the winning Triton kernel goes to ptxas, and everything from that point down happens at PTXAS’ default settings. The kernel autotuner’s search space is defined by what the kernel language can express, and no kernel language expresses “allocate registers differently”. This compiler control surface is a separate interface, exposed by ptxas itself starting from CUDA 13.3. It is imperative to mention that this exploration is genuinely hard. There are complex interactions between various compiler controls: a change to register allocation shifts occupancy, which changes whether a scheduling decision helps or hurts. The right setting is workload-specific, and there’s no universal answer to publish. And the payoff per unit of human effort is poor, which is exactly the profile of a problem one hands off to a search algorithm. The joint search: Helion Autotuner and PTXAS’ Advanced Controls Helion exposes the underlying compiler control space through two settings. Controls are packaged in an Advanced Control File (ACF, typically ending with .acf) which is a binary artifact applied at compile time, portable and versionable, that users can ship alongside their kernel. The first setting pins a known-good ACF as part of a config the user has already chosen: softmax_tuned = helion.kernel( config=helion.Config( advanced_controls_file="h100_example1.acf", block_sizes=[4], num_warps=8, num_stages=2, reduction_loops=[512], indexing=["pointer", "pointer", "tensor_descriptor", "tensor_descriptor", "pointer", "pointer"], ), static_shapes=True, )(_softmax) The second is a more interesting case. It hands a list of ACFs to Helion’s own autotuner and lets them be searched as just another dimension, alongside tile sizes and warp counts: softmax_search = helion.kernel( autotune_search_acf=[ "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_03.acf", "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_11.acf", "acfs/helion-booster-pack/candidate_17.acf", ], autotune_compile_timeout=120, static_shapes=True, )(_softmax) Two things are worth pointing out in this mode: The empty string is appended for you. Helion automatically adds “”, meaning “no ACF, compiler defaults”, to the list that is supplied. The default configuration is therefore always a candidate in the search, and the autotuner will only select an ACF if it actually won on measured time. The worst case of turning this on is that you spend some autotuning budget and get back the kernel you already had. That property is what makes it tempting to try on a kernel you care about. Sequential tuning finds a local optimum; this joint method doesn’t. This is the substantive argument for doing it in one loop rather than two. Suppose you autotune the kernel first, get block_sizes=[128, 128] with num_stages=4, and then go searching for compiler controls. You are now searching the control space conditioned on a kernel config that was itself chosen under default controls. But those dimensions are coupled through the hardware: block size and stage count determine register pressure and shared-memory footprint, and register allocation policy is precisely what decides whether that pressure causes spills. A control set that would shine at block_sizes=[64, 64] never gets evaluated there, because the kernel config was frozen before the compiler search began.The reverse ordering has the same problem. Searching both together is the only ordering that doesn’t have it, which is why autotune_search_acf lives inside Helion’s autotuner rather than being a post-processing step. The cost is search time. Each ACF multiplies the number of compile-and-measure trials, so this is not something to leave on by default for every kernel in a codebase. It is something to run once, offline, on a kernel that matters, and then pin the result with advanced_controls_file, exactly the way autotuned configs are pinned today. Where do these Advanced Control Files come from Now that we’ve understood the benefits of joint autotuning of Helion parameters with PTXAS’ advanced control files (ACF), the natural question one may have is how can these ACFs be generated. That is where NVIDIA’s CompileIQ comes into the picture. CompileIQ treats compiler-control selection as a hyperparameter optimization problem. It pulls a curated search space for the target compiler and toolkit version, then runs an evolutionary search: propose a population of candidate control sets, compile each one, check correctness against a reference, time the survivors, breed the winners, repeat. The output of this search process is an ACF file. There is nothing GPU-specific about the search algorithm itself, and the only GPU-specific parts are what is entirely in the objective function that the user writes, which is usually a few lines around triton.testing.do_bench. For most users however, the additional search budget is unnecessary, because the searching has been done. CompileIQ publishes Booster Packs – pre-tuned ACF catalogs – on its GitHub releases . The current helion-booster-pack contains 24 ACFs tuned across a range of Helion kernels, validated against ptxas from CUDA 13.4, targeting B200. So the realistic workflow for users is: download the pack, point Helion’s autotune_search_acf at it, autotune once, pin what wins. No search space to design, no objective function to write, no compiler expertise required! If you have a workload the pack doesn’t cover, pip install compileiq and run your own targeted search. That path is documented in NVIDIA’s CompileIQ blog post and in various CompileIQ examples . Helion and CompileIQ: Experimental Results This section highlights many possible ways in which one can run a CompileIQ optimization campaign on Helion kernels. As a sample case study we applied CompileIQ to the pretuned nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel, a Helion W4A4 (NVFP4 weight x NVFP4 activation) decode GEMV kernel that already ships a checked-in Helion AOT config for its target shape. The question: is there performance CompileIQ can extract below Helion’s own autotuning layer ,i.e., at the ptxas compilation stage? Environment and Methodology Benchmarking was conducted on a GB200 system with sm_100 (Blackwell, compute capability 10.0), utilizing ptxas 13.3.73 (CUDA 13.3), CompileIQ 1.0.3, Triton 3.8.0, and an editable source installation of Helion. All timing evaluations were executed via triton.testing.do_bench with the GPU clock locked. Every observed performance improvement was re-measured independently, validated against the PyTorch reference implementation for numerical correctness, and statistically filtered using a Welch’s t-test (p < 0.05) alongside Cohen’s d (d > 0.2). Complete statistical metrics are provided alongside each result below. Kernel Description nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel in helion/pretuned_kernels/nvfp4_gemv/nvfp4_gemv.py, computing out = (weight @ x) * alpha for a decode (one output row) GEMV. Both the packed NVFP4 weight and activation bytes are unpacked per K-group via hl.load_float4_e2m1fn_x16_to_float16, accumulated in fp16 over a 16-way static range, and scaled by a decoded E4M3 block scaler. This kernel includes a checked-in AOT configuration specifically for the N=8192, K=28672 “down_proj” decode-GEMV shape in _helion_aot_nvfp4_gemv_cuda_sm100.py: _CONFIG_FP4IN_DEFAULT = { "block_sizes": [4, 256], "num_warps": 2, "num_stages": 3, "range_multi_buffers": [None, True], } Using Runtime as CompileIQ Objective Function Using runtime as the CompileIQ objective function lets us optimize execution speed directly. The objective function takes a candidate ACF configuration, applies it to our fixed Helion kernel, and evaluates it: the kernel runs once, its output is checked against the PyTorch reference implementation, and only configurations that pass correctness are then benchmarked with triton.testing.do_bench. Any configuration that fails correctness returns an invalid score and is dropped from the search before it ever contributes a timing measurement. def objective(config) -> float: acf_path = ... # write `config` to a .acf, or None for baseline kernel = _make_kernel(acf_path) got = run() _check(got, ref, "fp4in", N, K) # correctness gate return do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean") We initialize a Search instance that couples our scoring routine to an evolutionary autotuner over PTXAS compiler controls, then invoke .start(). It sweeps candidate ACFs across generations generations of a pool_size-sized population, breeding the top-performing control configurations forward into each subsequent iteration. config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="min", generations=8, pool_size=15) tuner = Search( objective_function=objective, search_space=PtxasSearchSpace(version=cuda_version, variant="default"), search_config=config, dump_results="nvfp4_gemv_results.csv", worker_type=WorkerTypes.ISOLATED, # crashing ACF candidates shouldn't kill the search ) with gpu_benchmark_mode(clock_mhz=target_clock_mhz, raise_on_failure=False): results = tuner.start(task_timeout=60) Executing an evolutionary search with CompileIQ across PTXAS ACFs, spanning 8 generations with a pool size of 15 candidates over our fixed Helion configuration on GB200 yielded an optimized ACF control set. This candidate reduced execution time from a baseline of 0.0971 ms down to 0.0928 ms, delivering a 1.047x (4.7%) speedup as measured directly within the search’s scoring loop. sample baseline run: 0.09713 ms Best runtime (CompileIQ Search): 0.0928 ms Speedup: 1.047x Validation of CompileIQ Search Results To confirm our findings, every speedup is re-measured independently using increased warmup and repetition iterations under fixed GPU clock frequencies. Each configuration undergoes strict correctness verification against the reference model alongside a Welch’s t-test and Cohen’s d filter. This serves as our rigorous statistical threshold (requiring p < 0.05, cohens_d > 0.2, and optimized.mean < baseline.mean) to verify performance gains before trusting the numbers. # run 1 baseline: n=1744 mean=0.09752ms std=0.00218 optimized: n=2018 mean=0.09301ms std=0.00133 speedup_mean: 1.0485 p_value: 0.0 cohens_d: 2.501 significant: True # run 2 (independent re-run) baseline: n=1757 mean=0.09744ms std=0.00216 optimized: n=2028 mean=0.09299ms std=0.00130 speedup_mean: 1.0478 p_value: 0.0 cohens_d: 2.489 significant: True The two executions remain virtually identical within experimental variance: with d ≈ 2.5 demonstrating a massive effect size that easily surpasses our statistical threshold of 0.2 , verifying that this ACF performance gain is genuine. The two runs are virtually identical within experimental variance, and d ≈ 2.5 in both is a massive effect size nearly 12.5x past our d > 0.2 gate, confirming this ACF performance gain is genuine, not noise. Tuning against a hardware metric instead of runtime While execution speed is a common optimization goal, CompileIQ is not limited to runtime alone. Integrating directly with Nsight Compute (ncu) enables the objective function to target any hardware metric exposed by the tool. To determine the key architectural bottleneck limiting kernel performance, we start by evaluating its profile and analyzing nvfp4_gemv_fp4in_kernel on a GB200 system highlights the following bottlenecks: Section: GPU Speed of Light Throughput Memory Throughput % 78.99 L1/TEX Cache Throughput % 89.35 Compute (SM) Throughput % 37.29 Section: Occupancy Theoretical Occupancy % 25.0 Achieved Occupancy % 21.63 Est. Speedup: 21.01% ... theoretical occupancy (25.0%) is limited by the number of required registers. Profiling shows the kernel is register-limited. NCU’s own cost model attributes a 21% ‘Est. Speedup’ opportunity to occupancy, and this ceiling is set by register count, something PTXAS’s register-allocation controls can directly influence. Switching the objective from runtime to occupancy only touches two things: what the objective function scores, and the search’s problem_type: # objective(): do_bench(...) becomes an ncu metric read return _measure_occupancy(acf_path) # ncu: sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active # search config: minimize runtime -> maximize occupancy config = SearchConfiguration(problem_type="max", generations=4, pool_size=6) Pointing the search at achieved occupancy itself across 4 generations × pool size 6, rather than runtime, found a candidate that moved the proxy metric by +0.16pp (21.60% → 21.76% achieved occupancy, p = 9.2e-23, d = 13.17) and, independently re-measured, translated into a modest but statistically solid runtime win of ~1.75-2.0% (p = 3.6e-116, d = 0.78). Multi-Objective Tuning CompileIQ can also perform multi-objective tuning, where the scoring routine evaluates candidates along multiple dimensions simultaneously by returning a tuple rather than a scalar float. Instead of isolating a single top performer, the autotuning process maps out candidates along the Pareto frontier, identifying control sets that are not dominated across all target metrics. This yields a unified ACF optimized jointly for execution runtime alongside L1TEX cache throughput. def objective(config) -> tuple[float, float]: runtime_ms = do_bench(run, warmup=25, rep=100, return_mode="mean") l1_throughput = _measure_l1throughput(acf_path) return runtime_ms, -l1_throughput 8 generations × pool size 15 converged to a single dominant candidate on the Pareto front. Unlike a tradeoff curve, this single point beats every other evaluated candidate on both axes simultaneously in the search’s own scoring. Validating it on a fresh cache at shipping-grade trial counts: === RUNTIME (ms, lower is better) === p_value=3.516e-295 cohens_d=87.024 speedup_mean=1.0689x === L1TEX THROUGHPUT (%, higher is better; internally negated) === p_value=7.123e-19 cohens_d=3.686 baseline L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=81.5087% candidate L1TEX THROUGHPUT mean=85.9620% Multi-objective tuning found an ACF delivering a validated 6.9% runtime speedup, accompanied by a simultaneous 4.5pp L1TEX throughput gain (81.51% → 85.96%). Both results are statistically significant (p ≪ 0.05, Cohen’s d ≫ 0.2), with neither metric being traded off against the other. Joint ACF Optimization Across Multiple Input Shapes While earlier evaluations focused on a single kernel shape, N=8192, K=28672, real-world model deployment demands coverage across multiple configurations. The nvfp4_gemv implementation ships with several pre-tuned Helion AOT configurations, including a dedicated setup for N=15360, K=5120. Instead of maintaining distinct control files per shape, CompileIQ enables a unified search to discover a single, joint ACF that maximizes performance across both shapes simultaneously. def objective(config) -> tuple[float, ...]: """One shared ACF, one runtime score per shape (both minimize).""" acf_path = ... # write `config` to a temp .acf, or None for baseline return tuple(_bench_shape(acf_path, shape) for shape in SHAPES) Executing an 8-generation search with a pool size of 15 across both shapes yielded a Pareto front containing 4 optimal candidates: Candidate down_proj 15360_5120 pareto_0 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms pareto_1 0.0927 ms 0.0309 ms pareto_2 0.0944 ms 0.0308 ms pareto_3 0.0917 ms 0.0321 ms Compared to the default benchmark times of 0.0972 ms for down_proj and 0.0315 ms for 15360_5120, pareto_0 emerges as the standout configuration that consistently outpaces the baseline across both target tensor dimensions. To confirm these performance gains, we execute an independent validation of pareto_0 on each individual shape. Both configurations comfortably pass our statistical validation (1.05x speedup with a p-value of 1.1e-224 and Cohen’s d of 67.71 for down_proj, and 1.01x speedup with a p-value of 6.2e-73 and a d of 4.54 on the 15360_5120 shape), far exceeding our benchmark requirements and proving these gains represent genuine performance improvements rather than system noise. A single joint ACF successfully outperforms the default baseline across both target dimensions simultaneously. Applicability of this workflow for end-to-end model tuning While the focus of this entire post is about optimizing the underlying compiler for extracting more performance from individual kernels, it is important to zoom out and highlight how a workflow like this could be utilized for end-to-end tuning of models on PyTorch. The first step is to profile and characterize the most important kernels that are part of the model which you wish to optimize. Then, each of these kernels can then be a target of CompileIQ optimization, with an associated Advanced Control File to extract maximum performance from that instantiation of the kernel. These get applied during runtime using Helion’s pinned autotune configurations, using Triton’s ptxas_options API or directly via the PTXAS command line depending on the entry point of each kernel’s implementation. We want to be upfront about the expected gains: On kernels that are already highly optimized, compiler-control tuning has shown runtime improvements on the order of 2-7% which may still mean a lot for critical kernels in top models. Less optimized kernels have achieved double-digit performance gains, offering greater potential for meaningful end-to-end improvements. The important points to note are that it is found automatically, and requires little to no compiler expertise, it is verified against your own correctness check, and the result is a file you can commit next to the kernel and reapply on every build. It is the difference between a few percent that exists in principle and a few percent you actually ship. It also compounds exactly where you’d want it to. There are high-value kernels inside inference loops that run continuously across large fleets. Even a few percent at the bottom of the stack, applied to the operations that dominate a decode step, is valuable at that scale. Caveats ACFs are hardware- and toolkit-specific: An ACF tuned for sm_90 is not valid on sm_100. Applying a mismatched ACF can produce incorrect results or runtime errors, not just slower code. The booster pack manifest states its target architecture and toolkit version. This is also why the correctness check in the search loop is not optional. Search-time is a nontrivial cost: Every ACF in autotune_search_acf multiplies your autotuning trials. Use it offline on kernels that matter, then pin the winner. Gains are workload-specific: The result depends on the workload, the shapes, the architecture, and how much headroom the kernel has left. The only number that matters for your kernel is the one you measure on your kernel. Your turn to try this out! If you’ve never written a GPU kernel: start at pretuned_kernels/ . Pick something close to what you need, read it and then run it. The kernels are short, and they run at tuned speed immediately, with no autotuning wait. If you already use Helion: download the helion-booster-pack , add autotune_search_acf=[…] to one kernel you care about, and autotune it. The no-ACF baseline stays in the search, so the downside is bounded at the time you spend. See Helion’s examples/acfs/ for a worked example. If you work on kernels for a living: the takeaway here is not the tool itself. It is that the compiler’s control surface is a legitimate optimization space, it is searchable, and most people are not yet searching it. That is true of any compiler that exposes tunable controls, on any backend. We’re hopeful that we’ve inspired you to explore this space! Licensing Helion is open source and hosted by the PyTorch Foundation. CompileIQ is free to use and it is distributed under the NVIDIA Software License Agreement, a proprietary EULA. The ACF files it produces are freely distributable, which is why booster packs can be published and why an ACF can be committed alongside a kernel in an open repository. Links Helion https://github.com/pytorch/helion https://helionlang.com https://github.com/pytorch/hel

items.content: Featured projects Frontier models span language, video and audio, on architectures from dense and mixture-of-experts transformers to diffusion, state-space, world and structure-prediction models. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware. Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron , an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community. TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer , performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx, going live as public Beta on Oct. 20. “PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta Getting started: Easy device switching Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron') . # Run a training loop on Trainium model = MyModel().to('neuron') # the only change optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters()) for batch in dataloader: optimizer.zero_grad() loss = criterion(model(batch), targets) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") , after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") . # Run a compiled training loop on Trainium torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") # call once, before any compile model = MyModel().to('neuron') model.compile() # no backend argument optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters()) for batch in dataloader: optimizer.zero_grad() loss = criterion(model(batch), targets) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Capabilities TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn , torch.tensor , torch.autocast , torch.distributed , and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively. High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron ( details ). Eager Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience. torch.compile torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware. The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation. Ops and dtypes Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release. Distributed APIs Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather , reduce_scatter , all_reduce ) and the P2P APIs ( send , recv ) are supported. Collectives execute over Trainium’s dedicated collective cores intra-node and over the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) inter-node, so the communication transport is native to the hardware with no change to PyTorch APIs. Streams and Events Torch streams and events are supported natively. torch_neuronx.Stream and torch_neuronx.Event map PyTorch’s stream semantics onto Trainium’s hardware queues. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. The device-agnostic torch.Stream , torch.Event , and torch.accelerator entry points reach the same implementation, so code written against them runs unmodified. An error surfaces at the next synchronization point rather than at the operation that caused it; TorchNeuron tracks the earliest exception and re-raises it there with its original context. In execution, non-default streams multiplex onto a single hardware queue, so they keep ordering, priority, and event semantics but do not each get a dedicated engine; and when host collectives are disabled, a collective issued on a non-default stream keeps its place in that stream’s execution order but runs on the default hardware queue. Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) lets researchers and developers develop, optimize, and execute custom operators for both eager and torch.compile. Researchers can prototype ideas that require low level hardware control, including new model architectures. Developers can obtain finer performance control beyond Adaptive Eager and torch.compile by calling performance critical NKI kernels directly in model code to replace sequences of standard PyTorch operations (ATen ops). TorchNeuron also provides Trainium optimized, high-performance operators implemented with NKI and released open source as NKI-lib , covering mainstream LLM and multimodal scenarios for both dense and MoE models, such as FlashAttention and MoE blockwise kernels, which developers can use to improve performance on Trainium. The following example defines and registers a custom NKI operator using the PyTorch recommended register_autograd style: import torch import nki import nki.language as nl from torch_neuronx import nki_op # Declaring and implementing NKI kernels # Note in NKI kernels, the output tensor should be defined as parameter to the kernel @nki.jit def sin_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr): input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128]) output_tile = nl.sin(input_tile) nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile) return out_ptr # defining cos since it will be used in backward path of sin @nki.jit def cos_kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr): input_tile = nl.load(in_ptr0[0:128]) output_tile = nl.cos(input_tile) nl.store(out_ptr[0:128], value=output_tile) return out_ptr # after this line, there is no NKI code, just native PyTorch, registering custom ops @nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_sin", mutates_args={}) def pt_nki_sin(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: out = torch.empty_like(x) sin_kernel(x, out) return out @nki_op("mylib::pt_nki_cos", mutates_args={}) def pt_nki_cos(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: out = torch.empty_like(x) cos_kernel(x, out) return out def pt_nki_sin_backward(ctx, grad): x, = ctx.saved_tensors return grad * pt_nki_cos(x) # cos is derivative of sin def pt_sin_setup_context(ctx, inputs, output): x, = inputs ctx.save_for_backward(x) # Register backward pass and context function used during autograd for nki_sin pt_nki_sin.register_autograd(pt_nki_sin_backward, setup_context=pt_sin_setup_context) if __name__ == "__main__": x = torch.randn(128, 1, device="neuron", requires_grad=True) # Forward pass uses sin_kernel y = pt_nki_sin(x) # Backward pass, autograd calls uses nki_sin_backward() -> cos_kernel() loss = y.sum() loss.backward() Profiling with TorchNeuron TorchNeuron integrates with the standard torch.profiler.profile API extended with a NeuronConfig object that controls Neuron-specific data collection. This allows users to capture and correlate traces from framework-level CPU operations (PyTorch dispatch, Python stacks) as well as Neuron runtime and Trainium activity (controlled by NeuronConfig) enabling end to end performance analysis. Profiles captured can be visualized in the Neuron Explorer UI, where users can trace execution across framework, runtime, and device, jump from any event to the exact source line (source code viewer), navigate the workload through its call hierarchy (hierarchy viewer), and follow dependency chains to see what each stall is waiting on (dependency chain viewer). Neuron Explorer also emits a Parquet output with per-op and per-engine metrics, so the same data behind the UI can be queried directly or consumed by agents for automated bottleneck analysis. For programmatic access, users can work with the built-in torch.profiler tools. For example, the key_averages table lets users drill down into specific ops and use the sort_by argument to surface the device-side cost of each op, which is useful for identifying hotspots. Following code snippet shows an example ( details ): import torch from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity from torch_neuronx.profiling import NeuronConfig, ProfileMode, NeuronProfiler # Configure Neuron profiling and pass appropriate path as OUTPUT_DIR nc = NeuronConfig( modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME], profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR, capture_enabled_for_nc='0', correlate_device_time=True, ) # NeuronProfiler.export_trace() places the framework trace # in the same directory as Neuron system traces exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc) device = torch.device('neuron') x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device) weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device) def rms_norm_fn(t): x_sq = t * t mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6) return t * rms * weight # Profile your workload with torch.profiler.profile( activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1], experimental_config=nc, record_shapes=False, on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace, schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1), ) as prof: for step in range(4): with torch.no_grad(): _ = rms_norm_fn(x) torch.neuron.synchronize() prof.step() # Print the per-op summary, sorted by device time to surface hotspots print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4)) For additional capabilities and features refer to Neuron Explorer documentation . Customers and partners building on TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is already in use across startups, enterprises, ML industry partners, and academic institutions: spanning autonomous vehicles, robotics, video generation, speech, telecommunications, healthcare, and geospatial modeling. Below is a snapshot of what teams are building today. “Cartesia is building intelligence that learns from and interacts with the world the way humans do, starting with conversation. Our pioneering work on state-space architectures like Mamba powers Sonic (text-to-speech) and Ink (speech-to-text), the voice AI models behind conversational experiences that feel truly human. Real conversation demands three things at once: quality (naturalness and accuracy), efficiency (low latency at scale), and steerability. Most solutions deliver one or two. We designed our research and products from first principles to deliver all three, which means we need infrastructure that lets us squeeze maximum performance out of every layer without rewriting our stack. With PyTorch native support on AWS Trainium, we ran our standard inference pipeline with minimal changes to our PyTorch code. Small, fast ops map efficiently through the native path, so we didn’t have to hand-write kernels for them. That lets our team concentrate on writing high-performance NKI kernels for the layers that are called repeatedly and drive end-to-end latency. For real-time voice, every millisecond of network distance matters. Running on Trainium gives helps to put Sonic and Ink close to our customers globally.” Arjun Desai, Cofounder, Cartesia “Voice is becoming a first-class modality for AI, and Deepgram processes quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. To meet that demand, we need to scale efficiently while continuing to ship better models. Over a multi-month engagement, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center helped us port our model to PyTorch Native on AWS Trainium. In the benchmarks we evaluated, Trainium processes about 60% more input audio seconds per dollar than our existing GPU baselines, which helps us bring better models to customers at lower prices. We look forward to supporting future AWS AI chips in our solution.” Adam Sypniewski, CTO, Deepgram “Hugging Face is the leading open platform for AI builders, providing free access to over 6 million open models, datasets and applications through PyTorch-powered open-source libraries including Transformers and Diffusers. Until now, taking advantage of AWS Trainium required adapting Hugging Face models with Neuron-specific software and configuration; TorchNeuron makes Trainium a native backend for Transformers and Diffusers, so developers can use familiar model definitions through a fully open-source stack – a practical expression of our commitment to silicon neutrality and compatibility. It’s now easier than ever to deploy state-of-the-art open LLMs and the latest open image and video generation models on AWS Trainium, with TRL enabling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning and Neuron kernels delivering optimized performance automatically through our libraries.” Jeff Boudier, VP Product, Hugging Face Beyond these customers, we have been working with a number of partners who are building with TorchNeuron to enhance the Trainium ecosystem. These partners include Anyscale, Decart, Kernelize, Loka, Luminal, Makora, Modular, Nota AI, Radix, Wafer, and Yasp. How TorchNeuron Enables broader compatibility One of our goals with native PyTorch support is to enable developers to leverage the performance and cost benefits of Trainium while continuing to use the models, libraries, and workflows they already know. This helps preserve their investment in PyTorch, including their model code, inference and training infrastructure, debugging practices, and the community projects they build upon. The cost of running AI workloads includes the engineering time needed to get them working, optimize their performance, and maintain them as models and libraries evolve. We want developers to spend more time experimenting with architectures and improving model quality, and less time adapting their software to the underlying hardware. They should be able to start with a familiar model or training recipe, adapt it to their workload, and run it on Trainium with minimal changes specific to Neuron. TorchNeuron provides the foundation for this experience through compatibility with the broader PyTorch. TorchTitan Example TorchTitan is PyTorch’s native library for rapid experimentation and large-scale training. Its modular design makes it easier to customize training, test new ideas, and scale up experiments. TorchTitan trains on Trainium today. We continuously upstream into mainline TorchTitan, and torchtitan-neuron gives you those improvements before they merge, converging on mainline as each one lands. The Trainium-specific artifacts also ship in torchtitan-neuron and register through TorchTitan’s own extension points; those include NKI kernels, Trainium-tuned model configurations and training recipes, and profiling integrations for Neuron Explorer. # Install from source git clone https://github.com/aws-neuron/torchtitan-neuron cd torchtitan pip install -r requirements.txt # Download the llama3-8B tokenizer python scripts/download_hf_assets.py --repo_id meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --assets tokenizer --hf_token=... # Train Llama3-8B with Simple FSDP + torch.compile on a single trn2.48xlarge instance: export NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES=64 torchrun --nnodes 1 --nproc_per_node $NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint "localhost:0" \ -m torchtitan.train --module torchtitan_neuron.experiments.graph_trainer.llama3 --config simple_fsdp_llama3_8b \ --parallelism.tensor-parallel-degree 4 \ --parallelism.data-parallel-shard-degree -1 \ --training.global-batch-size 16 \ --training.local-batch-size 1 \ --compile.enable --compile.backend neuron Following is example loss curve of training Llama 3 8B on 8 x trn2.48xlarge with Tensor Parallel (TP) and Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel (HSDP) with TorchTitan Hugging Face Transformers v5 Transformers v5 is built for interoperability: one model implementation that runs on any platform and any hardware, and that downstream training and serving stacks consume directly. Trainium is a supported device upstream in the Hugging Face libraries, including Transformers, Diffusers, trl and kernels. Transformers v5 enables training and inference of text and audio models, Diffusers supports image and video generation, trl enables reinforcement learning of large language models, and NKI kernels are available through the Hugging Face kernels library. AWS and Hugging Face added the support to each library, so existing Hugging Face workflows run on Trainium with no device-specific code. Training. Transformers v5 strengthens full pre-training and fine-tuning readiness, with better initialization and compatibility with the parallelism and tooling ecosystem — TorchTitan for scale, Unsloth and TRL for post-training. Inference. Transformers v5 standardizes attention and kernels across model implementations. Diffusion. Tensor parallelism in Diffusers is merged upstream for Neuron, so image and video generation run through the diffusers APIs unchanged. Compatibility. Either way the weights load onto the device for training or inference, and the rest of the script is unchanged. Model coverage Blind Sweep (Broad testing at scale). We used the Hugging Face model universe to perform broad sweep across open source models. We continuously run 100k Hugging Face models that cover 99.9% of real-world usage (based on the download count). We ran each model on Trainium in a reduced but representative configuration and record what happens: does it load, does the forward and backward pass run, does it compile, and which operators executed on the device versus fell back to CPU. The following graph shows the result of 100k model run across eager and torch.compile mode as of September, 2026. We are working on closing the remaining gaps, targeting closing most, if not all, in future releases. The August 2026 run produced about 154K test outcomes, of which roughly 69K were skipped with a valid reason: About 30K of those are skipped by PyTorch own eligibility checks (for example CUDA-only and CPU-only tests) and are not Neuron-specific. PyTorch is where AI research happens, where the models are defined, and increasingly where production happens too. Researchers want to experiment and innovate, and customers want the performance AWS Trainium offers to enable them to achieve their performance and scale goals. The training and serving libraries are written against PyTorch’s own APIs, and new libraries and new versions ship continuously. Over the last several years, PyTorch made those APIs accelerator-agnostic, with official extension points for registering custom hardware. Today, to address the growing demand from the developers and research community on Trainium, we are excited to share an even simpler approach to program the chip as a standard PyTorch device, ahead of its open source launch at PyTorch Conference North America on Oct. 20. AWS Trainium is a portfolio of AI chips designed from the ground up for next generation cloud scale AI training and inference. We are announcing TorchNeuron , an open source native PyTorch backend for Trainium, so the model code, the libraries, and the tools you already use run on Trainium. This integration builds directly on the accelerator-agnostic extension points, including the PrivateUse1 device backend and torch.accelerator APIs, created by the PyTorch community. TorchNeuron supports eager execution for research and debugging including new adaptive eager mode with improved performance, torch.compile for production performance, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for custom kernels, on Trainium2 and Trainium3. Also, with Neuron Explorer , performance engineers use the same torch.profiler to trace execution from framework to hardware, linking every event back to its source line to pinpoint bottlenecks and optimize efficiently. TorchNeuron will be released as open source under Apache 2.0 at github.com/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx, going live as public Beta on Oct. 20. “PyTorch’s vision is straightforward: developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms. Native support for AWS Trainium expands that choice, enabling researchers and engineers to experiment and iterate using the eager execution and distributed APIs they already know. Teams can take advantage of Trainium’s capabilities without reinventing their workflows or leaving the PyTorch ecosystem.” – Jana van Greunen, Director of PyTorch Engineering at Meta Getting started: Easy device switching Getting started is straightforward. Run your code on Trainium using the pointer: .to('neuron') . # Run a training loop on Trainium model = MyModel().to('neuron') # the only change optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters()) for batch in dataloader: optimizer.zero_grad() loss = criterion(model(batch), targets) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Modern code written against torch.accelerator, PyTorch’s recommended device-agnostic API, runs unmodified. A compiled model needs the Neuron backend named, once with torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") , after which torch.compile(model) takes it, or per call as torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") . # Run a compiled training loop on Trainium torch.compiler.set_default_backend("neuron") # call once, before any compile model = MyModel().to('neuron') model.compile() # no backend argument optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters()) for batch in dataloader: optimizer.zero_grad() loss = criterion(model(batch), targets) loss.backward() optimizer.step() Capabilities TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PrivateUse1, PyTorch’s official extension point for custom hardware, so the standard APIs work as written: torch.nn , torch.tensor , torch.autocast , torch.distributed , and torch.profiler all operate on the neuron device. The two execution modes of PyTorch, eager and torch.compile work natively. High-level architecture diagram of TorchNeuron ( details ). Eager Eager runs operations immediately, so Python control flow, prints, and breakpoints all work with no compile or trace step. This is the mode for research and debugging. Eager mode dispatches operations individually. Executed directly, each operation compiles its own Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) file, launches it on device, and moves its intermediates through HBM. We are also introducing adaptive eager mode (experimental), to reduce the launch cost and provide better opportunities to fuse operations to approach performance of compiled graph without a code change, while retaining the interactive experience. torch.compile torch.compile(model, backend="neuron") captures the model into a graph the Neuron compiler optimizes, and is the mode for stable, high-performance models moving to production. torch.compile can be used to optimize the whole or part of the model and works seamlessly with eager mode. FlexAttention is supported natively. TorchDynamo captures the model into an FX graph, AOTAutograd traces the backward graph ahead of time, the Neuron backend lowers the result, by way of Torch-MLIR, into StableHLO, and the Neuron compiler produces a NEFF file that executes on hardware. The Neuron inference stacks are built on the same torch.compile support in TorchNeuron. vLLM Neuron is a plugin to vLLM and serves LLMs; vLLM Omni Neuron is a plugin to vLLM Omni and serves diffusion models for image and video generation. Ops and dtypes Broad aten operator coverage for ops seen across text, multimodal and vision language, image and video generation and understanding, state space models, and world models. Models can use BF16, FP32, and FP16, with integer and boolean types, and torch.autocast and mixed precision code operate as written. TorchAO and FP8 are currently supported under private Beta and will be made generally available in the next release. Distributed APIs Distributed inference and training can use the standard PyTorch APIs and the high-level parallelism modules compose with your model as written: DDP, FSDP2, SimpleFSDP, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, along with common compositions like FSDP2 with tensor parallelism, ZeRO that are essential for training large models. DTensor and DeviceMesh are supported to handle sharding and the multi-dimensional process groups. The collective APIs (example: all_gather , reduce_scatter , all_reduce ) and the P2P APIs ( send , recv ) are supported. Within a stream, data movement and computation stay in order automatically. Separate streams carry no implicit dependency on one another, so across streams you make that ordering explicit by recording an event on the producing stream and waiting for it on the consuming stream before using the result. Developers can use libraries such as TorchTitan, which brings together PyTorch’s distributed and compilation capabilities for large-scale training, and Hugging Face Transformers, which provides access to community model implementations, pretrained checkpoints, and APIs for adapting models to their applications. TorchTitan Example TorchTitan is PyTorch’s native library for rapid experimentation and large-scale training. Its modular design makes it easier to customize training, test new ideas, and scale up experiments. TorchTitan trains on Trainium today. We continuously upstream into mainline TorchTitan, and torchtitan-neuron gives you those improvements before they merge, converging on mainline as each one lands. The Trainium-specific artifacts also ship in torchtitan-neuron and register through TorchTitan’s own extension points; those include NKI kernels, Trainium-tuned model configurations and training recipes, and profiling integrations for Neuron Explorer. # Install from source git clone https://github.com/aws-neuron/torchtitan-neuron cd torchtitan pip install -r requirements.txt # Download the llama3-8B tokenizer python scripts/download_hf_assets.py --repo_id meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --assets tokenizer --hf_token=... # Train Llama3-8B with Simple FSDP + torch.compile on a single trn2.48xlarge instance: export NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES=64 torchrun --nnodes 1 --nproc_per_node $NEURON_RT_NUM_CORES \ --local-ranks-filter 0 --role rank --tee 3 \ --rdzv_backend c10d --rdzv_endpoint "localhost:0" \ -m torchtitan.train --module torchtitan_neuron.experiments.graph_trainer.llama3 --config simple_fsdp_llama3_8b \ --parallelism.tensor-parallel-degree 4 \ --parallelism.data-parallel-shard-degree -1 \ --training.global-batch-size 16 \ --training.local-batch-size 1 \ --compile.enable --compile.backend neuron Following is example loss curve of training Llama 3 8B on 8 x trn2.48xlarge with Tensor Parallel (TP) and Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel (HSDP) with TorchTitan Hugging Face Transformers v5 Transformers v5 is built for interoperability: one model implementation that runs on any platform and any hardware, and that downstream training and serving stacks consume directly. Trainium is a supported device upstream in the Hugging Face libraries, including Transformers, Diffusers, trl and kernels. Transformers v5 enables training and inference of text and audio models, Diffusers supports image and video generation, trl enables reinforcement learning of large language models, and NKI kernels are available through the Hugging Face kernels library. AWS and Hugging Face added the support to each library, so existing Hugging Face workflows run on Trainium with no device-specific code. Training. Transformers v5 strengthens full pre-training and fine-tuning readiness, with better initialization and compatibility with the parallelism and tooling ecosystem — TorchTitan for scale, Unsloth and TRL for post-training. Inference. Transformers v5 standardizes attention and kernels across model implementations. Diffusion. Tensor parallelism in Diffusers is merged upstream for Neuron, so image and video generation run through the diffusers APIs unchanged. Compatibility. Transformers v5 is a native backend of runtime libraries such as TorchTitan, vLLM and SGLang, extending their model breadth to most of the 3 million public models available on Hugging Face. We are working on enabling and validating this integration on Neuron, bringing this expanded model support to Trainium instances. Loading a model onto Trainium from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", # Neuron hardware is automatically detected device_map="neuron" ) TorchNeuron registers Trainium through PyTorch’s PrivateUse1 extension point, which puts Neuron in PyTorch’s device enumeration. device_map=”auto” finds it with no configuration, and device_map=”neuron” names it explicitly. Either way the weights load onto the device for training or inference, and the rest of the script is unchanged. Testing methodology and results Our testing methodology included verifying TorchNeuron on broad model coverage across HuggingFace and TorchTitan models, and PyTorch upstream test suite across both eager and torch.compile mode. Model coverage Blind Sweep (Broad testing at scale). We used the Hugging Face model universe to perform broad sweep across open source models. We continuously run 100k Hugging Face models that cover 99.9% of real-world usage (based on the download count). We ran each model on Trainium in a reduced but representative configuration and record what happens: does it load, does the forward and backward pass run, does it compile, and which operators executed on the device versus fell back to CPU. The following graph shows the result of 100k model run across eager and torch.compile mode as of September, 2026. We are working on closing the remaining gaps, targeting closing most, if not all, in future releases. PyTorch Upstream tests We run the PyTorch upstream test suites: ATen, Dynamo, distributed, and profiler, and report the pass rate against the enabled tests. The August 2026 run produced about 154K test outcomes, of which roughly 69K were skipped with a valid reason: About 30K of those are skipped by PyTorch own eligibility checks (for example CUDA-only and CPU-only tests) and are not Neuron-specific. The remaining ~39K are deliberate Neuron skips, in three groups Operators without a native Neuron lowering at this point (~22K, the largest group; ties to operator coverage above that we plan to close in sequential releases) – corner cases for elementwise, reduction, foreach, advanced-indexing, and advanced-linalg operators, and fused LSTM/GRU cells. CUDA-specific tests (i.e. the upstream eligibility check did not flag) – CUDA graphs, NCCL-specific collectives, CUDA-specific Dynamo paths tests are skipped with eligibility check. Features TorchNeuron explicitly chose not to support in the first release as customers didn’t request them: composite-operator compliance, sparse tensors and sparse ops, NestedTensor, forward-mode autograd (JVP), arbitrary attention masks in native multi-head attention (no-mask and causal are supported), per-channel quantization, negative/conjugate view bits, torch.signal windows, bilinear/bicubic up sample, and dynamic and symbolic shapes

items.content: At a glance Challenges a core assumption in robotics AI: Our research shows that running physical AI inference exclusively on onboard GPUs can limit robot performance, battery life, and scalability, and that offloading inference to edge or cloud GPUs can offer significant advantages. Demonstrates measurable benefits of inference offloading: Across representative mobile manipulation workloads, offloading improved task success rates, enabled larger AI models, and helped robots respond more effectively in dynamic, real-world environments. Extends robot operating time: Replacing power-hungry onboard AI compute with lightweight onboard hardware and remote inference can substantially improve battery life, enabling robots to operate longer between charges. Introduces a new capability in the Physical AI Toolchain: Developers can now containerize, deploy, and orchestrate robotics AI workloads across robots, edge infrastructure, and the cloud using Kubernetes-based tooling for distributed inference. Readily-available physical AI, with robotics assisting users in manufacturing, home, and warehouses scenarios, holds immense potential to improve safety, productivity, and assistance across a wide range of tasks. In many ways, AI for the physical world represents a major frontier for AI . Physical AI must operate in open, unpredictable environments, interact with both other robots and people, and work with a diversity of embodiments. Realizing this vision requires advances along three dimensions: robot hardware, embodied AI models, and systems infrastructure for training and inference. While robot hardware and the AI models have advanced rapidly in recent years, we turn our focus on a relatively under-addressed aspect: inference infrastructure of physical AI . Enabling robots to effectively and safely operate in the physical world will require sophisticated systems to handle large volumes of distributed inference compute. Today, the prevailing approach to physical AI is to provision a GPU onboard the robot, e.g., by wiring a GPU to the robot. In this model, the robot’s inference will be confined to the onboard GPU, and provide the robot with the necessary chunks and sequence of actions for the execution of its tasks. While higher-level planning may be performed in the cloud, task execution typically remains tied to the robot itself. We challenge this assumption. As physical AI models grow in size and sophistication, the constraints of onboard compute become increasingly apparent. GPUs consume significant power, reduce battery life, add cost and weight, and can limit the ability to run the latest generation of AI models. To better understand the systems implications of physical AI, we conducted the first systematic study of robotics workloads. We focused on mobile robotic manipulation , with the canonical task such as “check for rubbish in the kitchen and put it in the trash.” Such a task involves planning the path to the kitchen, perceiving the environment to find rubbish, navigating to the rubbish, picking up the rubbish, and navigating back to the trash can for disposal. We evaluated representative models across three core capabilities: semantic mapping and planning, navigation, and manipulation, as summarized in Figure 2. Figure 2: Details of the models used for the different components of mobile manipulation. Offloading physical AI inference out of the robot improved its response time and accuracy, along with battery lifetime and cost. We evaluated the inference models across a range of onboard, edge, and cloud compute configurations. Details of the specific test hardware are available in our technical report . Benefits in task performance : Our evaluation shows offloading inference can significantly improve robot performance across mapping, planning, navigation, and manipulation workloads. Some smaller GPUs could not accommodate the mobile manipulation stack. On GPUs with sufficient memory, mapping and planning slowed by up to 383% compared to an A100, thus limiting the robot’s abilities in dynamic spaces. Navigation showed a 30% drop in its timely detection of obstacles with lighter GPUs. While the VLA models did not dramatically slow down with smaller GPUs, the slowdown was still sufficient to drop their accuracies by 50%. In other words, onboard GPUs limited the performance of the robots while offloading their inference to an on-premise or cloud GPU boosts their operations, as shown in the videos below and quantified in the graphs. As physical AI models continue to grow in size and complexity, the benefits of offloading are likely to become even more pronounced. Figure 3a: The video shows the handover task with onboard GPUs. Figure 3b: The video shows the handover task when the inference is offloaded. Figure 4: Success rates of robot arms handing over objects to each other when inference is performed with different GPUs (some onboard, and some offloaded). Offloading improves success rates. Benefits in battery lifetime : Beyond performance, onboard GPUs also significantly drained the battery life of the robot. We compared the increase in battery lifetime by replacing an onboard GPU with a Raspberry Pi-5 board and shipping all the data to the offloaded GPU. The larger onboard GPUs, such as Jetson Thor, drained robot batteries by up to 160% (or a few hours) for even the larger robots. Figure 5: Impact of offloading GPU inference on the battery life of the robots; the above numbers are for the Stretch-3 robot. The above results show that offloading GPU inference out of the robot is critical for functioning in the open world with large models and long battery lifetimes. Nonetheless, offloading inference out of the robot involves a complex tradeoff involving performance, network latency and bandwidth, and available GPU resources. We believe that our measurement study will inform the design of physical AI inference systems. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab Toolset for automatic offload We have built a toolset for easy inference offloading out of the robot and distributing inference between the edge GPU and cloud. Kubernetes is a natural platform to provide a uniform abstraction to distribute robotic AI between the robot’s compute, edge GPU, and overflowing to the cloud. The toolset allows automatic containerization and offloading of robotics workloads using declarative specifications, distributes physical AI containers with smart policies using Kubernetes, and integrates with robotic simulators, LeRobot, and ROS2 for easy development. The sequence of steps below shows how the toolset can be prompted with what to offload, and how it creates a separate container for GPU inference and offloads the same. Figure 6: Steps in the offloading toolset with containerization and deployment. Microsoft has recently released the Physical AI Toolchain (opens in new tab) for operationalizing physical intelligence at scale. Physical AI Toolchain is an open-source, production-ready framework that integrates Microsoft Azure (opens in new tab) cloud services with NVIDIA’s (opens in new tab) physical AI stack, accelerating robotics and physical AI developers to automate and scale data curation, augmentation, and evaluation across perception, mobility, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning pipelines. We are announcing the addition of an industry-first capability for offloaded physical AI inference for robots as part of the Physical AI Toolchain. This release includes example projects for offloading inference of a SO-101 and a UR10e. The videos below show the offloading of the inference of Microsoft’s Rho model , targeted at dual-arm robots, to a Jetson Thor GPU, which controls the actions of the Mobile Aloha robot (opens in new tab) . Figure 7a: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to press the blue button. Figure 7b: Offloading of GPU inference of Microsoft’s Rho model controlling the Mobile Aloha robot for interactions with the BusyBox to turn the knob to position 4. Check out the inference offload feature, look into the source code, and let us know your feedback. We have already tested it with many real-world use cases, and look forward to hearing about your deployment experiences. items.content: At a glance Harnessed Agentic RL: Microsoft Research Asia introduces a training paradigm in which the same agent harness used in deployment participates directly in reinforcement learning, removing the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. Lightweight by design: Agent Lightning v1.0 delivers a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code. Native Kubernetes support: agents run as standard Kubernetes jobs on self-managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, with no dependency on paid commercial sandbox services. Data-efficient training recipe: an end-to-end coding agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5-9B from 41.8% to 56.4% Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage point gain, using only about 6,000 training samples based on open sourced dataset. AI agents have evolved from single models to complex full-stack systems built from models, tools, and execution environments. Their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an approach where AI systems learn through trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties for their actions. RL can make those agents better, but most agent RL systems require developers to reimplement the agent inside the training framework. That is costly, and it means the agent being trained is not quite the agent that gets deployed. To address this, researchers at Microsoft Research Asia have introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open-sourced a fully rebuilt Agent Lightning v1.0 (opens in new tab) . Compared with the original, Agent Lightning, v1.0 puts more emphasis on staying lightweight, on integrating with real harnesses, and on a complete, reproducible agent RL training pipeline. Agent Lightning v1.0 was rebuilt around Harnessed Agentic RL, with key improvements: Lightweight : the entire framework is about 3,500 lines of code. Agent Lightning v1.0 implements a complete Harnessed Agentic RL system in a codebase that is small and clear enough to understand, modify, and extend. Training on a real agent harness : agents reach the model through the large language model (LLM) proxy in Agent Lightning v1.0, leaving existing harness code unchanged. Native Kubernetes support : agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, without external commercial sandbox services. Self-managed clusters and local infrastructure alike can support rollouts at scale. A complete coding agent training example : an end-to-end pipeline built on Qwen3.5-9B raised Pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8% to 56.4%, an absolute gain of 14.6 percentage points, using only about 6,000 training samples. The limits of traditional agentic RL Traditional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop with the environment. In a ReAct-style loop, the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, the observation is appended to the context, and the model generates the next action, so the whole rollout maps onto one continuous token trajectory. Early RL systems such as verl, AReaL, and slime were built this way, which meant training an agent required rebuilding its loop inside the RL framework. Real harnesses have outgrown that assumption. Coding agents such as mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Codex each bring their own context management, tool protocols, execution logic, and dependencies, as do general-purpose agent systems. Rebuilding one for training is expensive, and the rebuilt agent may no longer behave in the same way as the deployed agent. Agent Lightning takes a different route. It places an LLM proxy between the agent and the model. The agent continues to run as before: simply point the endpoint that previously called the model API at Agent Lightning, and the training framework can observe and record its model calls. In v1.0, the researchers go further and formally define this paradigm as Harnessed Agentic RL: whichever agent harness is used in deployment is the harness that takes part directly in reinforcement learning during training (Figure 1). Figure 1. Traditional agentic RL compared with Harnessed Agentic RL. In traditional agentic RL, the training framework manages the environment and the agent loop. In Harnessed Agentic RL, the harness manages both. Four challenges in training with real harnesses A core difference between Harnessed Agentic RL and traditional agentic RL is that the environment interaction loop is handled by the agent harness rather than the training framework. The training system can only observe a series of LLM request and response pairs, so a single rollout may be split into a variable number of training samples.
